rv.q: After snoozing through many well-meaning tracts about Iraq, the prospect of a play about a financial meltdown wasn't appealing. But 'Enron' is a whip-smart, edge-of-your-seat ride that'd rival anything at Six Flags -- there are even raptor-headed businessmen prancing around.

Playwrights aren’t usually conversant with concepts of high finance, and most of us theatergoers prefer it that way. But this British import, written by Lucy Prebble and directed by Rupert Goold, turns out to be one of the most vibrant new offerings on Broadway this season.
Even if Enron isn't the last word on the free market debacle, it is a fantastic theatrical event.
The British import 'Enron' is a theatrical roller coaster that captures the dizzying rise and fall of the energy company with inventive staging and compelling performances.

Industry doomsayers were all wet about 'Enron.' This London bombshell is both a dazzling piece of entertainment and a gripping cautionary tale about the criminal chicanery that eviscerated the most respected corporate body in America.
But for all its undeniable inventiveness, the play is curiously uninvolving.
If only the play were as dramatically satisfying.
If Enron's stock were still circling the ticker, my advice would be to buy, buy, buy.

Despite the serious research and the playful imagination, the splendid new American cast and the irresistible craven puppets, the play tells us what it is in the first half-hour and then tells us again for another two hours.

Yet even with a well-drilled cast that includes bright Broadway headliners like Norbert Leo Butz and Marin Mazzie, the realization sets in early that this British-born exploration of smoke-and-mirror financial practices isn’t much more than smoke and mirrors itself.
The problem with 'Enron' is that it tries to be too many things at once and winds up being none of them particularly well.

With Goldman Sachs executives answering to a Senate committee this week, the latest round of financial wizards under fire after being accused of corrupt practices, perhaps the Enron scandal of 2001 seems like yesterday's news. Not so, argues the young British writer Lucy Prebble.
Without manipulation or fraud, "Enron" the play earns a very "Strong Buy."
Prebble's writing and the production dreamed up by director Rupert Goold are stunning enough to provide steady wonder, involvement and delight.
Jeffrey Keith Skilling, the former president of Enron Corp., has been quietly serving a 24-year sentence at a federal prison in Colorado.
Too often, in fact, Enron plays like 60 Minutes on acid.
Her play is like a big, shiny, beautifully wrapped package that once eagerly ripped opened reveals a horde of Styrofoam peanuts through which you search vainly for the anticipated present.
The play has a harder time becoming a taut work of modern theater.
Rupert Goold's slick, aggressive production maintains a chaotic energy level mixed with playful theatricality:
The actor is equally delightful here, but then Skilling is the play's most fully realized character in a work more concerned with plot than people.
